title: media-list: a watchlist that beats a spreadsheet
spec:
OBJECTIVE
A local, private web app that holds everything Evan means to watch — anime, movies, live action — and makes deciding what to watch next enjoyable rather than administrative.

WHY (the sponsor's own framing)
Evan already knows how to keep a list; he has explicitly rejected the way. 'I want to do it in a way that is more fun than an excel sheet.' The spreadsheet is not failing at storage, it is failing at RETRIEVAL and DESIRE: a row of text does not make you want to watch the thing. So cover art, a browsable wall, and a spin-the-wheel picker are not decoration on top of the requirement — they ARE the requirement. Any ticket that ships correct data behind a dull surface has missed the objective.

SUCCESS SHAPE
1. Adding a title is search-and-pick, never data entry. Type a few words, see posters, click one; title, year, kind, summary, artwork and IMDb link all arrive on their own. If a user is ever asked to type a summary or paste an image URL, this has failed.
2. The home page is a wall of cover art with a carousel you rotate by click-and-drag AND by side buttons. It should be pleasant to just look at.
3. One global ordered queue, filterable by kind (anime / movie / live-action), reorderable by hand.
4. A spin-the-wheel picker with a genuinely good animation, for when Evan cannot decide. The motion quality is in scope, not polish to be dropped.
5. A whole series is ONE item. No episode or season tracking — explicitly declined at intake.
6. Watching something means giving it 1-5 stars; it then moves into a browsable Seen archive that stays worth visiting.
7. CSV import is a RESOLVER: loose rows (title, optional year/kind/why) get searched against TMDB, shown as candidate matches with posters, disambiguated by Evan, then committed. Evan has no existing list and intends to generate one with a chatbot, so the importer must tolerate exactly that kind of loose input. CSV export is full fidelity and re-imports exactly.
8. The look is swappable via repo-tour's skin contract — one scoped CSS file plus one registry row — so a whole new style can be one-shotted later.
9. The database creates itself on first startup. No migration step, no server to install.
10. The repository is public; the contents of the list are not. DB, cached title artwork and exports never enter git.

CONSTRAINTS SET BY THE SPONSOR
- Stack: FastAPI + Vite + SQLite. Deliberately small — 'It is not a big project.'
- Loopback only, 127.0.0.1:7799 (reserved in PROJECT_PORTS.md). Phone access is deferred to the GUTS Bridge and is NOT built here.
- MIT licensed, github.com/BMA-Corgea/media-list.
- Data: TMDB for artwork/metadata/IMDb ids, AniList for anime specifics, Pexels for ambient chrome only — never title art.

NON-GOALS (named so they are not smuggled in)
Episode/season progress. Multi-user or sharing. Streaming-availability lookup. Recommendations engine. Mobile-specific UI. Anything bound wider than loopback.

dir-clarify.evidence: CLARIFIED IN CONVERSATION, 2026-09-04. Eight direction-level questions were put to Evan and all eight were answered directly, in his own words: (1) search-and-pick confirmed as the add flow; (2) localhost only, phone deferred to GUTS Bridge; (3) one global queue organizable by genre, plus a spin-the-wheel with a good animation; (4) a whole anime is one item, episode splitting explicitly declined; (5) 5 stars into a Seen archive; (6) carousel driven by click-and-drag AND side buttons; (7) reuse repo-tour's modular skin approach; (8) FastAPI + Vite + SQLite, MIT, github.com/BMA-Corgea/media-list, DB self-creating, CSV import+export. Follow-ups also settled: repo renamed medita-list -> media-list at his instruction; TMDB key supplied and verified live; privacy boundary (DB/art/exports out of git) proposed and accepted; no pre-existing list, so import must resolve loose chatbot-generated rows. Goal restated to him twice across the conversation and corrected by him where wrong (he narrowed scope on 2 and 4). SPONSOR CONFIRMATION: 'Noted. ... please get to work on this' — an explicit go. RESIDUAL UNKNOWNS ARE REFINEMENT-ALTITUDE, NOT DIRECTION-ALTITUDE, and are deliberately left to each child ticket's own spec gate: exact carousel physics/easing, wheel animation choreography, whether Seen items can be re-queued, and what the title page shows beyond summary/hero/IMDb link. None of these can change the ticket set.

dir-scope.evidence:
EPICS SCOPED WITH BOUNDARIES + SEQUENCING (presented to Evan in full before filing).
FOUNDATION: T-2 skeleton/self-creating SQLite/skin contract (produces: a booting app on 7799, a DB, the token+component layer every surface depends on; consumes: nothing).
DATA SPINE: T-3 TMDB+AniList service and artwork cache (produces: search->candidates-with-posters, details->full record, art cached to data/art/; consumes T-2).
CAPTURE: T-4 search-and-pick add flow (produces: titles in the queue, the interaction every later capture surface reuses; consumes T-3).
BROWSE: T-5 carousel wall, T-6 title page, T-7 queue ordering + kind filters (each consumes T-4; each independently acceptable — a reviewer can reject the carousel and keep the title page).
DECIDE + CLOSE: T-8 spin-the-wheel (own gate because the animation quality is a stated requirement, not polish), T-9 review + Seen archive (consumes T-6).
DATA IO: T-10 CSV export + resolver import (consumes T-7 for queue positions; the highest-risk ticket — bulk writes into Evan's data).
DRESS: T-11 Pexels chrome + credits.json (consumes T-5; last because it needs surfaces to dress).
Sequencing edges become --after at dir-route. Non-goals named and excluded rather than buried: episode/season tracking, multi-user/sharing, streaming availability, recommendations, mobile UI, any bind wider than loopback.
EXCEPTION QUESTION: asked once, in the sponsor's own words, and answered — recorded as grant G-1 (epic T-1, gates '*', scope_confirmed true) with his verbatim quote.
